text: Once you suspect a leaked credential has been escalated, you need to prove exactly what happened, in what order, with which identity. That proof lives in CloudTrail and the Azure Activity Log — but only if you know which fields actually matter and which log stream you're supposed to be reading in the first place.

Every CloudTrail event is a JSON record, and during an investigation you pivot on a handful of fields. userIdentity.accessKeyId ties a given action to the exact credential that was used — which matters, because a single IAM user can hold more than one key, and only one of them might be the one that leaked. sourceIPAddress separates normal automation traffic from an unfamiliar IP showing up mid-sequence. eventName and requestParameters tell you precisely what changed — in this example, AdministratorAccess being attached to a service account that should never need it.

Not every CloudTrail event is logged the same way. Management events — control-plane calls like AttachUserPolicy or RunInstances — are on by default and cover almost everything in a typical escalation sequence. Data events, covering S3 object-level access and Lambda invocations, are off by default because of cost and volume; turn them on for anything sensitive, because without them you can't prove which objects were actually touched. CloudTrail Insights adds anomaly detection on top, flagging unusual call volume a simple rule would miss.

Azure trips up more investigators, because people treat 'the Azure logs' as one thing. They're not. The Activity Log records control-plane operations against Resource Manager, with a correlationId that chains related calls together. Azure AD sign-in logs are a completely separate stream covering authentication — Conditional Access outcomes and risk level. Azure AD audit logs cover directory changes, like a new secret added to a service principal, which is exactly where last lesson's Application Administrator abuse would actually show up.

A real investigation pivots across all three. The sign-in log shows an authentication from an unfamiliar location. The audit log shows a new secret added to a privileged app right afterward. The Activity Log shows that app then assigning itself a broader role. Export all three into one Log Analytics workspace or Sentinel so they're queryable together in KQL, instead of chasing three separate blades in the portal one at a time.

With the evidence pinned down — which credential, which API calls, in what order — you're ready to act on it. Next, we cover containment: how to isolate exactly the compromised identity or resource these logs point to, without taking down anything else in the account or subscription.
